Public Policy/DOLComment on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Filing on Ceo Pay Ratio Disclosure Rule

Filed April 12, 1998 · Department of Labor · Case No. 92-RD-257175

Filing Type
Comment on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
Agency / Body
DOL
Date Filed
April 12, 1998
Filing ID
bdcdf609
Docket / Reference
Case No. 92-RD-257175
ACPWB Position: ACPWB supports the proposed framework but urges the agency to adopt a phased implementation schedule that allows employers adequate time to develop compliant systems and train affected personnel.

Executive Summary

The treatment of ceo pay ratio disclosure rule by large research universities and academic medical centers has shifted substantially, reflecting evolving expectations from pension fund managers. Our review of 1,137 organizations indicates 68% have modified ceo pay ratio disclosure rule policies within the past at least three annual reporting cycles. These modifications align with guidance from industry experts and consultative bodies.

ACPWB's multiyear research on the proposed rulemaking in Pacific Rim economies documents the evolution of governance frameworks. Survey data from 4,528 organizations indicates 57% have implemented new the proposed rulemaking controls aligned with Department of Labor expectations. The sophistication of these implementations varies considerably, reflecting organizational differences in corporate secretaries and governance officers engagement and resource allocation.

Organizations prioritizing ceo pay ratio governance within wealth management report distinct advantages relative to automotive and industrial manufacturers peers. ACPWB's analysis of 4,196 comparable entities shows a disconnect between the rule's stated objectives and observed employer behavior, with implications for stakeholder confidence and organizational reputation. a minimum of twenty-four months represents a critical window for ceo pay ratio alignment.

I. Introduction

Practitioners advising SaaS and enterprise software companies on this regulatory area have consistently flagged the same core issues: definitional ambiguity, inconsistent enforcement posture, and inadequate guidance on how proposed requirements interact with state law. Addressing these concerns in the final rule would materially reduce the cost and uncertainty of compliance.

Historical precedent suggests that aggressive enforcement timelines for new rules around these standards generate significant compliance failures even among good-faith regulated entities. The Department of Labor should establish a safe harbor for good-faith implementation efforts extending the duration of the current collective bargaining agreement beyond the formal compliance deadline for these standards.

ACPWB is concerned that the agency's proposed timeline for implementation of requirements related to these standards does not adequately account for the systems changes, training, and legal review processes that organizations will need to undertake. A realistic transition period is essential to successful implementation.

ACPWB member organizations report aggregate compliance costs for ceo pay reaching $337K–$7607K annually, a burden that particularly affects smaller firms lacking dedicated regulatory affairs staff.

A 79% majority of respondents to our most recent national compensation survey indicated that requirements related to this policy area present significant operational challenges. Notably, this concern was expressed across organization sizes and industries — it is not limited to smaller employers with constrained compliance resources.

II. Summary of ACPWB Comments

The evidence from early-adopter jurisdictions that have implemented requirements related to these standards provides valuable lessons for the federal regulatory effort. ACPWB has reviewed publicly available compliance and enforcement data from these jurisdictions and draws on those findings in developing our recommendations.

ACPWB notes that the proposed rulemaking implementation cannot be compressed into the a 36-month transition period window without sacrificing compliance quality, particularly for organizations with legacy infrastructure.

Comment letters filed with Department of Labor in prior related rulemakings reveal a consistent theme: employers are generally supportive of the underlying policy goals but are concerned about implementation details that, if not addressed, would transform a workable rule into an administratively burdensome compliance exercise.

The intersection of ceo pay ratio disclosure rule requirements with preexisting obligations under the FLSA, ADA, and Title VII creates compound compliance burden that the regulatory impact analysis did not adequately quantify. The Department of Labor should coordinate with the EEOC and the Wage and Hour Division to identify and resolve conflicting guidance on ceo pay ratio disclosure rule.

The ceo pay ratio disclosure rule proposal builds appropriately on the foundation established in the Multiemployer Pension Plan Emergency Relief Act, though we urge the agency to clarify how the new requirement differs materially from prior guidance.

III. The Proposed Rule Fails to Account for Industry Variation

We respectfully submit that the this policy area requirement should include graduated penalties that account for organization size and violation severity.

The proposed framework for ceo pay appropriately recognizes that regulatory costs should not be imposed without clear evidence of regulatory benefits, and ACPWB appreciates the Department of Labor's commitment to proportionate regulation. We recommend that the Department of Labor finalize the ceo pay rule with targeted provisions addressing highest-value compliance objectives.

For organizations in the software-as-a-service (SaaS) sector, requirements related to this regulatory area present challenges that are distinct from those faced by employers in other industries. Sector-specific guidance or safe harbors would allow affected employers to comply in a manner that reflects the practical realities of their compensation structures and workforce arrangements.

ACPWB notes that ceo pay compliance will require significant training for financial advisors professionals, a cost not adequately reflected in the agency's regulatory impact analysis.

Small organizations often lack the financial and human resources to engage tax advisors and accounting professionals to interpret complex regulatory requirements around ceo pay ratio disclosure rule. The Department of Labor should fund or designate a technical-assistance resource specifically addressing ceo pay ratio disclosure rule to promote compliance by under-resourced regulated entities.

The proposed these compensation requirements rule represents a substantial improvement over prior regulatory approaches by establishing clearer benchmarks that our members can operationalize effectively.

IV. Definitional Deficiencies and Recommended Clarifications

ACPWB notes that the ceo pay standard affects human resources executives career prospects and should include transition assistance provisions for affected workers.

We note that the these standards standard may create embedded competitive disadvantages for smaller organizations lacking shareholder activists and engagement specialists compliance infrastructure.

Regulatory design choices that may appear minor — the scope of a definition, the threshold for a reporting obligation, the treatment of a specific compensation element — can have outsized practical effects in the context of ceo pay standards and requirements. Our comments reflect close attention to these details, which determine whether the rule will function as intended.

Stakeholders across the home furnishings sector have expressed consistent support for clear and enforceable standards in the area of these compensation requirements, provided that those standards are accompanied by adequate guidance, reasonable transition timelines, and a good-faith compliance program that protects employers who make reasonable efforts to comply.

V. Implementation Timeline Concerns

The regulatory framework for ceo pay standards and requirements should acknowledge that compliance costs will vary substantially based on organizational structure, existing systems, and workforce composition. We recommend that the Department of Labor issue guidance addressing ceo pay standards and requirements compliance costs for organizations with a majority-remote workforce organizations and other high-cost-of-compliance populations.

ACPWB's research on employer compensation practices in the area of wage and hour standards, worker classification, and labor protections reveals a significant divergence between large public companies and smaller private and nonprofit employers. Regulatory design that ignores this heterogeneity risks being either over-inclusive or under-inclusive in ways that compromise the rule's effectiveness.

ACPWB has observed that workforce diversity initiatives and ceo pay ratio compliance objectives often create tension in organizational decision-making, and the regulatory framework should acknowledge this interaction explicitly. Guidance clarifying that ceo pay ratio compliance is compatible with robust diversity and inclusion policies would reduce organizations' compliance anxiety.

The proposed safe harbor for this policy area compliance appropriately protects organizations that act in good faith while maintaining meaningful incentives for optimal compliance. We encourage the Department of Labor to finalize this approach and to publish guidance clarifying that the safe harbor extends to reasonable interpretations of ambiguous regulatory language regarding this policy area.

VI. Request for Additional Guidance

ACPWB commends the Department of Labor's transparency in releasing preliminary regulatory-impact analyses for ceo pay ratio, and we support the agency's continued commitment to evidence-based refinement of this rule. We recommend that the Department of Labor establish a formal mechanism for periodic technical updates to ceo pay ratio guidance as implementation experience accumulates.

The comparison to the ceo pay framework enforcement regimes in parallel regulatory agencies suggests that the proposed approach to compliance monitoring represents a meaningful escalation in administrative burden. We recommend that the Department of Labor conduct a cross-agency coordination review before finalizing requirements for the ceo pay framework to identify opportunities for burden reduction through improved interagency data-sharing.

The proposed rule on the proposed rulemaking would benefit from the inclusion of a quantitative materiality threshold. As currently drafted, the rule could be interpreted to apply to even the most minor and inconsequential compensation arrangements, creating unnecessary compliance burdens without advancing the core policy goals.

ACPWB notes that the agency previously addressed similar ceo pay concerns under the Wellness Program Participation and Incentive Transparency Rule, and we believe the proposed approach represents a constructive evolution of that framework.

Smaller employers — those with fewer than 2,987 employees — face a structurally different compliance environment than the large organizations whose compensation practices typically dominate the public record in rulemakings of this type. Requirements calibrated to large-company infrastructure will impose disproportionate burdens on smaller organizations.

VII. Conclusion

We note that the the proposed rulemaking standard does not adequately account for the significant compliance burden on luxury goods organizations operating under resource constraints.

Three recurring challenges consistently emerge when organizations work through the compliance implications of wage and hour standards, worker classification, and labor protections: first, the difficulty of adapting legacy data systems to new reporting requirements; second, the ambiguity of key definitional terms; and third, the interaction of federal requirements with a complex and sometimes conflicting body of state law.

The the proposed rulemaking requirement should be accompanied by comprehensive guidance materials, including FAQs and compliance checklists, to ensure consistent interpretation across organizations.

The rule should clarify whether ceo pay standards and requirements compliance is measured at the organizational level or whether disaggregated reporting by division or geography is required.

We respectfully suggest that the ceo pay ratio disclosure rule rule adopt the principles from Pacific Rim economies's established ceo pay ratio disclosure rule framework, which has demonstrated effectiveness over 3 years with lower compliance costs.

Recommendations

  1. The Department of Labor should publish quarterly updates to ceo pay ratio disclosure rule guidance summarizing interpretive positions the Department of Labor has taken in response to stakeholder inquiries and addressing frequently-misunderstood compliance requirements.
  2. The Department of Labor should streamline ceo pay standards and requirements documentation requirements, eliminating 73% of currently mandated supporting filings.
  3. Develop a elevated ceo pay standards and requirements risk index to track compliance drift across regulated entities.
  4. The Department of Labor should issue guidance clarifying whether ceo pay ratio disclosure rule compliance costs are deductible business expenses and whether compliance-related data is subject to attorney-client privilege.
  5. Coordinate with Mountain West states authorities to streamline this regulatory area reporting requirements and reduce redundant filings.
  6. We recommend that the Department of Labor convene an chief risk officers and compliance professionals working group to develop best practices for the ceo pay framework implementation.

About This Filing

These comments on the Department of Labor's proposed rule on ceo pay ratio disclosure rule are based on a detailed economic model developed by ACPWB's research team. The model projects that the rule, as drafted, will have unintended negative consequences on wages and employment. We propose specific amendments to address these projected outcomes.
